title: Monte Cassino
hook: Benedict founds his monastery and writes a Rule for beginners

segments.voice: Yesterday, Benedict in the specus at Subiaco, fed with bread on a rope. Your line was away from rome.

Listen. That's the first word. Not pray, not obey, not work. Listen, my son, to the teachings of the master, and bend the ear of your heart. That's how Benedict opens the short book monks and nuns would live by long after him. He wrote it on a mountain called Monte Cassino, where he'd come with his monks after years of building small communities around Subiaco.
screen: `THE FIRST WORD: LISTEN.` → `THE EAR OF YOUR HEART.` → `A BOOK ON A MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Gregory the Great tells how Benedict came to Cassino. On the height stood an old temple to Apollo, where country people still offered sacrifice. Benedict broke the idol, built two chapels in its place, one to Saint Martin and one to Saint John the Baptist, and preached to the people around, calling them to faith. A mountain of old worship became a mountain of prayer. Next, the Rule. Gregory says Benedict wrote a rule for monks, outstanding for its discretion and clear in its language, and that anyone who wanted to know how Benedict lived could find it there, because he couldn't have taught otherwise than he lived. What's in it? A day built from prayer, work and reading. Monks gather to sing the psalms at set hours, day and night. They work with their hands. They read. They eat together and listen to reading at meals. The abbot is told to remember he'll answer to God for every one of them, and to adjust to the weak as well as the strong. The Rule even tells the abbot to call everyone to counsel, because God often reveals what is better to the younger. Now the line that gives us today's carry. In the last chapter, Benedict calls his own work a little rule for beginners. Not a masterpiece: a beginning, written so people could start. He points beyond it to the scriptures and the Fathers for anyone who wants to go higher. Benedictine monks and nuns still live by it today, and on Monte Cassino, monks still pray.
screen: `A TEMPLE BECOMES CHAPELS.` · `A RULE CLEAR AND WISE.` · `PRAYER, WORK, READING.` · then, large: `A LITTLE RULE FOR BEGINNERS.`

segments.voice: Hear the first line again, gently: Listen, my son, to the teachings of the master, and bend the ear of your heart; Benedict wrote it to a son, so hear it however it reaches you. Then bring to mind one person whose words you heard this week with only half an ear, and go back over what they said slowly, as if for the first time, without answering it or fixing it. If you pray, ask to hear God, and that person, with the ear of your heart.
Monte Cassino. The mountain where Benedict built his monastery on the site of an old temple and wrote his Rule, which begins with the word listen. Today's word.
Your line: a little rule for beginners. Beginners are exactly who it was written for. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns live by the Rule of Saint Benedict, praying the psalms together at set hours, working and reading, and some communities read a passage of the Rule aloud each day.

chat.says: Is Benedict's Rule a strict rulebook for spiritual experts?
options: No: he called it a little rule for beginners, and pointed to scripture for more.
Yes: it was written for monks who had mastered prayer and wanted a harder path.
No: it's a short list of punishments, with nothing on prayer, work or reading.

notes: Rule, Prologue 1: 'Ausculta, o fili, praecepta magistri, et inclina aurem cordis tui' — rendered in my own plain English, no modern translation quoted. Confirm.

Rule 73: 'hanc minimam inchoationis regulam', pointing to scripture and the Fathers. Rule 3: abbot calls all to counsel because the Lord often reveals what is better to the younger. Rule 2: the abbot answers for the souls in his care and adapts to each. Paraphrased; confirm.

Dialogues 2.8: temple of Apollo on Cassino, idol broken, oratories of Saint Martin and Saint John, preaching to the people. Dialogues 2.36: rule 'discretione praecipuam, sermone luculentam', he could not teach otherwise than he lived. Confirm.
